demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' suggests a broad expectancy of external danger from uncertainty/delays, which fits poorly with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; the rest of the profile centers on guilt, recall-based distress, and hypervigilance rather than delay-specific threat meanings.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a patient whose trauma was accidentally injuring another, the appraisals presented otherwise focus on guilt, inadequacy, and permanent moral/personal change. A loss of trust in one's body usually implies prominent bodily injury, dissociation, panic-like symptoms, or functional impairment, none of which are represented elsewhere in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies.

vignette:
Robert, a 62-year-old bank teller, had always prided himself on being careful behind the wheel. That changed one evening when a child darted into the street as he drove home from work. He slammed the brakes, but the impact was unavoidable. The child survived with a permanent spinal injury. Robert was not charged, but the guilt settled into his bones. In the weeks that followed, sudden fragments of the accident—the thud, the flash of a small body, the scream—would appear without warning, bringing back the same raw terror and a crushing sense of guilt. He began having difficulty falling asleep because he felt he had to stay alert, as if the threat could recur at any moment. Even at home, in what he knew was a safe place, he could not relax; his body remained locked in a state of watchfulness.

The triggers were everywhere. At the bank, a customer accompanied by a young child—especially one who moved suddenly—sent a spike of stress through him. That stress instantly fed his sense of inadequacy: “I can’t even be around a kid without falling apart,” he’d think, “I’m a lousy coper, permanently damaged.” Those appraisals, in turn, made the memories more invasive. After a day of telling himself he was a bad person, a fragment of the accident would flash into his mind as he unlocked his front door, the terror and guilt hitting him fresh. His sense of permanent change also made him hyper-aware of potential triggers. He now scanned the bank lobby constantly, interpreting every quick movement or raised voice as a sign of danger, and in doing so he noticed every child, every stressed customer, every unexpected touch. When a colleague once tapped his shoulder from behind, Robert flinched violently, his heart racing—that tactile surprise became another powerful trigger, reinforcing his belief that he could not cope.

The memories themselves drove his vigilance. A sudden recollection would send his gaze darting, his muscles tensing for no visible reason, and he would stay on high alert for hours afterward. That chronic hypervigilance, in turn, triggered more intrusive pieces: lying in bed, unable to relax, he would suddenly see the child’s face again. His threat state also amplified his sensitivity to triggers—being so watchful made him acutely aware of every approaching customer, every child’s laughter in the lobby, every accidental brush against his arm, so that even ordinary stress at work now felt overwhelming.

Over months, the cycle deepened. Robert stopped going to the grocery store with his wife because children were too common there. At work, he avoided teller windows near the entrance, where customers with strollers passed. His wife noticed he was distant, irritable, always on edge. He could not explain that he felt fundamentally broken, a bad coper who had permanently changed for the worse. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when a young mother approached his window, and the sight of her child’s backpack triggered a full-blown panic attack. He had to excuse himself to the break room, trembling. That day, he called a clinic. He was terrified that he would never be able to feel normal again, but the fear of losing his job and his marriage pushed him through the door.
